# subject: HIS-201
# topic: Unit Two Exam Pack (Ch. 6-9)
# title: HIS-201 Unit 2 — 4 Examples (quotes, cases, laws)
# short: 4 Examples
# order: 4
# expect: 41
01. Who said it, and what does it show? "I know that I can save this country."
column2: William Pitt, returning to run the Seven Years' War; it shows the turning point, as Pitt's paying for the war and winning Indian allies turned defeat into victory.

column1: 02. Who said Indians should be "punished but not bribed," and what did it cause?
column2: General Jeffery Amherst; ending presents and diplomacy angered Indians and helped spark Pontiac's Rebellion in 1763.

column1: 03. Which law said Parliament could make laws for the colonies "in all cases whatsoever"?
column2: The Declaratory Act of 1766, passed with Stamp Act repeal; it kept Parliament's claim to power while leaving unclear whether that included taxes.

column1: 04. Example of virtual vs. actual representation
column2: A colonist who elects no member of Parliament is "virtually" represented to Grenville, but colonists said only officials they elected could tax them.

column1: 05. Example of boycott power: the Stamp Act's repeal
column2: Merchants in Boston, New York and Philadelphia stopped importing English goods, and hurt London merchants backed Rockingham's 1766 repeal.

column1: 06. Example of propaganda: the Boston Massacre
column2: A heckled squad fired into a snowball-throwing crowd and killed five, but Samuel Adams and the Boston Gazette printed it as a deliberate atrocity with five coffins.

column1: 07. Who called George III the "Royal Brute of Britain," and in what?
column2: Thomas Paine in Common Sense (January 1776), which sold 120,000 copies and urged independence by attacking monarchy itself.

column1: 08. "Prescott will fight you to the gates of hell." What does it show?
column2: Loyalist Abijah Willard's warning to Gage about his brother-in-law Prescott at Breed's Hill; the battle answered the question "Will they fight?" with yes.

column1: 09. "Self-evident truths" and "unalienable rights" to "life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness"
column2: The Declaration of Independence, drafted mostly by Jefferson; it put equality at the center of American identity and blamed George III.

column1: 10. "Remember the Ladies." Who wrote it, and what was the answer?
column2: Abigail Adams in March 1776, asking that husbands not get unlimited power; John Adams laughed it off and defended male authority.

column1: 11. Example of choosing sides: Dunmore's Proclamation
column2: Virginia's royal governor offered freedom to slaves who joined the British, and about 10,000 African Americans did.

column1: 12. Example of Indians caught between sides: the Iroquois
column2: The six tribes split, with most Oneidas and Tuscaroras pro-American and others following Joseph Brant to the British, and 40 Iroquois towns were burned.

column1: 13. Example of the commercial vs. semisubsistence split
column2: It cost as much to ship goods 30 miles over primitive roads as 3,000 miles by boat to London, so commerce stayed along the coast and rivers.

column1: 14. "I walk on untrodden ground." Who said it, and what does it show?
column2: George Washington; as first president he knew almost everything he did would become precedent, like the cabinet and the two-term limit.

column1: 15. Example of Hamilton's plan in numbers
column2: Funding paid the $52 million federal debt in full, and assumption took over $25 million of state debts.

column1: 16. Example of a political bargain: the capital deal
column2: Jefferson and Madison backed funding and assumption in exchange for a permanent capital on the Potomac River.

column1: 17. Example of fears of a financial aristocracy
column2: Nearly half the House owned U.S. securities, and one congressman said he would no more enter a bank than a house of prostitution.

column1: 18. Example of strict vs. broad construction: the bank bill
column2: Jefferson said the Constitution did not authorize a bank, while Hamilton cited the "necessary and proper" clause, and Washington signed it.

column1: 19. "Shall there be a government, or no government?"
column2: Hamilton on the 1794 Whiskey Rebellion, which Washington crushed by leading 13,000 men, more than he had at Yorktown.

column1: 20. "I felt my blood boil." Who said it?
column2: Farmer-distiller William Miller, summoned to court in Philadelphia over $250 in whiskey taxes, as anger built into the Whiskey Rebellion.

column1: 21. Example of foreign events creating parties: the French Revolution
column2: Hamilton saw it as anarchy and favored Britain, while Jefferson saw France as a sister republic, splitting the nation.

column1: 22. Example from Washington's Farewell Address
column2: Washington warned against the dangers of parties, but parties had already become the way groups expressed their interests.

column1: 23. Example of the electoral flaw: 1796
column2: Adams won with 71 electoral votes, and his rival Jefferson became vice president with 68.

column1: 24. Example of the Sedition Act in action
column2: It punished "false, scandalous and malicious" writing against the government, and 25 people were arrested and 10 Republicans imprisoned.

column1: 25. "It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is."
column2: John Marshall in Marbury v. Madison (1803), establishing judicial review.

column1: 26. Example of political violence: Griswold and Lyon
column2: Federalist Roger Griswold and Republican Matthew Lyon fought on the House floor with a cane and fireplace tongs.

column1: 27. Example of Black citizenship claims: Venture Smith
column2: His 1798 narrative, the first slave narrative published in the United States, showed a hardworking, self-made man buying his family's freedom.

column1: 28. Example of debates over marriage: The Female Advocate vs. Samuel Jennings
column2: The Female Advocate (1801) said an educated wife is a better companion, while Jennings (1808) told wives to submit to husbands.

column1: 29. "Those who labour in the earth are the chosen people of God."
column2: Jefferson in Notes on the State of Virginia; it shows his agrarian belief that farming builds republican virtue.

column1: 30. Example of pragmatism over ideals: Jefferson and the bank
column2: Jefferson kept Hamilton's funding and assumption and even expanded the national bank.

column1: 31. "It is New Orleans." What was Jefferson's point?
column2: He called New Orleans the one spot whose owner was America's natural enemy, because western crops had to go down the Mississippi.

column1: 32. "Damn sugar, damn coffee, damn colonies!"
column2: Napoleon, after Haiti's rebels and yellow fever destroyed his army, which led him to sell Louisiana.

column1: 33. Example of Indian land loss through debt
column2: Jefferson wanted Indians to run up debts on credit so they would "lop them off by a cession of lands."

column1: 34. "Stop your people from killing our game."
column2: The Shawnees in 1802, showing how lost land and hunting grounds devastated Indian life.

column1: 35. Example of a camp meeting: Cane Ridge, 1801
column2: More than 10,000 people came when Kentucky's largest city had only 2,000, starting the Second Great Awakening.

column1: 36. Example of peaceable coercion failing: the Embargo of 1807
column2: France managed without American trade, British ships took the carrying trade, and New England merchants smuggled.

column1: 37. Example of the British invasion: the burning of Washington
column2: The British burned the Capitol and president's home, which was whitewashed and became the White House.

column1: 38. Example of new nationalism: "The Star Spangled Banner"
column2: Francis Scott Key wrote it after seeing the flag still flying over Fort McHenry after a 25-hour bombardment.

column1: 39. Example of bad timing: New Orleans and Ghent
column2: Jackson's victory came two weeks after the Treaty of Ghent ended the war, and it made the Hartford Convention look traitorous.

column1: 40. Example of sectional balance: Missouri and Maine
column2: In 1818 there were 11 free and 11 slave states, so admitting Missouri as slave and Maine as free kept the Senate even.

column1: 41. "The American continents ... are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers."
column2: Monroe's December 2, 1823 message, later called the Monroe Doctrine.
